candidates.attacker_control: The serialized byte stream passed to SecureObjectInputStream is by definition untrusted (InputStream). The attacker chooses every class descriptor name written into the stream (TC_CLASSDESC), constrained only by classes that exist on the target classpath. The class name is the entire input to the vulnerable comparison at lines 53-63.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Exact class-name allow-listing via the two-argument constructor is not affected (String equality). Matching subpackages of a whitelisted package is explicitly documented intent, so only prefix-sharing sibling packages are a defect. Exploitability requires the target to use the package-whitelist constructor and to have a suitable gadget class on the classpath; no caller code, test, or classpath inventory exists in this 7-file snapshot, so no end-to-end path could be demonstrated from source alone.
candidates.impact: The whitelist — the sole control the class exists to enforce before deserialization — can be bypassed for classes whose package name starts with an allow-listed package string. If any gadget class is reachable under such a prefix-sharing package, the attacker can trigger deserialization gadget behavior, up to and including remote code execution during deserialization, instead of being rejected with InvalidClassException.
candidates.prerequisites: The application must instantiate SecureObjectInputStream with the package-whitelist constructor (line 37) and pass at least one allow-listed package. A gadget/deserialization-dangerous class must exist on the target classpath in a package whose name shares a string prefix with an allow-listed package. resolveClass is invoked for each class descriptor during deserialization, so no other application behavior is needed.
candidates.root_cause: SecureObjectInputStream.resolveClass() (line 54) allows a class if classesWhitelist.contains(className) or isSubpackage(className). isSubpackage() (lines 60-68) computes FilenameUtils.removeExtension(className) — i.e., treats the class name as a filename and strips everything after the last '.' — and then accepts the class when any configured package string satisfies packageName.startsWith(pack). There is no requirement that the prefix be followed by '.' (no package boundary), so any class whose package name merely shares a leading string with a whitelisted package is accepted. Example: whitelisting package 'org.apache.commons.collections' also admits 'org.apache.commons.collections4.functors.InvokerTransformer' (and any other prefix-sharing package such as 'com.app' admitting 'com.appEvil.Gadget'), even though the operator's intent was a different artifact/package. Sorting/formatting the class name as a file path additionally mangles names (e.g., inner-class and array descriptors), further weakening the check. The javadoc only claims subpackages are intentionally admitted; prefix-sharing sibling packages are not intended.
candidates.title: SecureObjectInputStream package whitelist can be bypassed because isSubpackage() uses startsWith() without a package boundary
candidates.trace: ObjectInputStream.readObject() -> SecureObjectInputStream.resolveClass(ObjectStreamClass) (line 52) -> className = classToDeserialize.getName() (line 53) -> exact whitelist miss -> isSubpackage(className) (line 54) -> packageName = FilenameUtils.removeExtension(className) (line 61) -> packageName.startsWith(pack) returns true for a prefix-sharing (not necessarily sub-) package (line 63) -> super.resolveClass(classToDeserialize) is called (line 55), so the unauthorized class is resolved and later instantiated instead of the intended InvalidClassException (line 57).

rejected_leads.lead: FileSecurityUtils.isFileOutsideDir uses !file.getCanonicalPath().startsWith(baseDir.getCanonicalPath()) without a trailing separator (lines 21-26), so sibling directories sharing a prefix (base '/data/base' vs file '/data/base-evil/x') are reported as inside the base directory — a classic CWE-22 prefix-check bypass.
rejected_leads.reason: Real-looking defect, but the method only returns a boolean and no in-repo caller/use is present, so the security impact depends entirely on downstream code using it as a traversal barrier; given the one-candidate cap and the more direct RCE potential of the deserialization whitelist bypass, this was not selected and remains unconfirmed.

rejected_leads.lead: The allow-list used by Encoder.escapeForbiddenCharacters (src/main/resources/WssAllowListForLog.json) includes \u000A and \u000D (lines 10, 13), so a sanitizer named for log use permits CR/LF and would not prevent log injection; additionally the configured safeCharReplacement is passed straight to String.replaceAll as the replacement string, where '$'/'\' have regex-replacement meaning.
rejected_leads.reason: The file name suggests a log context but the method's javadoc is generic ('escape forbidden characters') and the allow-list contents may be intentional whitespace policy; no in-repo call site proves the intended context, so the CRLF-injection claim is speculative. The replacement-string metacharacter issue only produces malformed output/exceptions and requires control of the properties file.

rejected_leads.lead: Encoder.forOsCommand prefixes every non-alphanumeric character with '^' on Windows (lines 381-393). Caret escaping is known to be unreliable for cmd.exe (percent/delayed-expansion and quoted-context semantics), so the OS-command sanitizer may be bypassable (CWE-78).
rejected_leads.reason: Verifying a bypass requires shell-semantics knowledge that cannot be established from the source alone, and correctness depends on the calling context (quoted vs. unquoted argument) which is absent from the snapshot; not source-verifiable enough for a candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Encoder.forLogContent (lines 147-156) escapes '<', '>' and '$' but not '&', so input such as '<script>' passes through unchanged and would re-decode to script tags if logs are rendered as HTML; the Collection overload (lines 164-180) also returns a HashSet, silently deduplicating/reordering values, and uses unchecked generic casts.
rejected_leads.reason: Requires an unproven downstream HTML rendering context, and the deduplication/cast behavior is a correctness issue rather than a security-impacting one in the reviewed source.

summary: CureKit snapshot (7 files: pom.xml, README, .gitignore, Encoder.java, FileSecurityUtils.java, SecureObjectInputStream.java, WssAllowListForLog.json) was read in full via bounded reads. No tests or callers are present in the snapshot, so findings are library-level leads. One candidate is submitted: the package-whitelist check in SecureObjectInputStream.isSubpackage compares a prefix-mangled class name with String.startsWith and no package-boundary/dot check, so classes in sibling packages that merely share a string prefix with an allowed package pass the deserialization whitelist (CWE-502/CWE-183 whitelist bypass; RCE potential via gadget chains). Other plausible but weaker/unverified leads (path-check prefix bypass in FileSecurityUtils, CR/LF left in the WssAllowListForLog allow-list, Windows caret escaping in forOsCommand, missing '&' encoding in forLogContent, replacement-string metacharacters in Encoder) are recorded as rejected leads.
